# Asteroids That Collide

**Stack** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/asteroid-collision/)

> Everything about this problem is on this page: the question, what the input
> promises, the hints, the long explanation, every approach in Python, Java and C++,
> and a script you can run. It **does not hide anything** — if you are partway
> through the journey for this problem, it will show you the ending.

Each value is an asteroid: its magnitude is the size and its sign the direction, positive moving right and negative moving left. Asteroids move at the same speed, so a collision happens only when a right-mover is immediately followed by a left-mover. The smaller one is destroyed; equal sizes destroy each other. Return the state once no more collisions can happen.

## What the input promises

- 2 <= asteroids.length <= 10^4
- -1000 <= asteroids[i] <= 1000, and never 0
- a collision needs a POSITIVE on the left and a NEGATIVE on the right — two asteroids moving the same way never meet
- equal magnitudes destroy each other, so both disappear rather than one surviving

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `asteroids = [5, 10, -5]` | `[5, 10]` | 10 destroys −5, then nothing else can meet. |
| `asteroids = [8, -8]` | `[]` | Equal sizes annihilate. |
| `asteroids = [10, 2, -5]` | `[10]` | −5 destroys 2, survives, then meets 10 and loses. One arrival caused two collisions. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Which asteroid does a new left-mover meet first? The most recently surviving right-mover.
2. That is a stack. Push right-movers; a left-mover has to fight its way down through them.
3. One arrival can destroy several — so the fight is a loop, not a single comparison.

</details>

---

## Understanding the Problem

Picture a single lane of traffic frozen in a photograph. Each car is a number: the size of the number
is how heavy it is, and the sign is which way it is pointing — positive means it is driving right,
negative means it is driving left. Everything then starts moving at the same speed. A crash can only
happen in one arrangement: a car driving **right** with a car driving **left** somewhere ahead of it.
Two cars pointing the same way never meet, and a left-mover with a right-mover ahead of it is two cars
driving apart. When two do crash, the heavier one continues unharmed and the lighter one is gone; if
they weigh the same, both are gone.

Report the lane once nothing can crash any more.

**The core question:** which asteroids survive, given that one arrival can set off a **chain** — a
left-mover that destroys its neighbour is still travelling, so it immediately meets whatever was
behind that neighbour. The naive approach is slow because it resolves one crash and then rescans the
whole lane from the beginning to find the next, paying a full pass per crash.

### The constraints, and what each one unlocks

| Constraint | What it unlocks |
|---|---|
| `2 <= asteroids.length <= 10^4` | Ten thousand elements with an `O(n²)` fallback is a hundred million operations — slow but survivable, which is why the **repeated-sweep** baseline can actually be run and used as the oracle. At least two elements, so there is no empty case. |
| `-1000 <= asteroids[i] <= 1000`, never 0 | Sizes are small and, crucially, **zero is excluded** — so `sign` is always well defined and "not moving" is not a case. Magnitudes fit anywhere; nothing here needs big integers or overflow care. |
| A collision needs a **positive on the left and a negative on the right** | This is the permission slip for the whole document. Only one adjacency out of four can ever crash, so a right-mover can be filed away as "safe for now" the instant it is read, and the only thing that ever reopens the question is a left-mover arriving later. |
| Equal magnitudes **destroy each other** | The case that breaks naive code. Two other outcomes leave exactly one survivor; this one leaves none, and the newcomer must stop fighting **without being pushed**. Nearly every wrong solution to this problem is wrong here. |

Note what is *absent*: nothing says survivors get reordered or renumbered. The answer is always a
**subsequence of the input, in the original order, with the original values** — which is what makes the
final in-place rung possible.

The worked example used in every section below:

```
asteroids = [10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]        answer: [-12]
```

It is chosen because it contains all three collision outcomes and one cascade: the `-5` fights twice,
the `-12` clears the lane, and the `-8` annihilates with the `8`.

### The case analysis, before any code

This problem is not an algorithm you discover; it is a table you write down and then transcribe. Write
it first and the code is mechanical. Write the code first and you will ship the equal-magnitude bug.

| What is on top of the survivors | What arrives | Do they meet? | Outcome | What the newcomer does next |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| anything | a **right**-mover | no — they drive apart or the same way | — | it joins the survivors |
| nothing (empty), or a **left**-mover | a left-mover | no — nothing ahead is coming back | — | it joins the survivors |
| a right-mover, **lighter** than the newcomer | a left-mover | yes | the top is destroyed | **keep fighting** — the next one down may also be a right-mover |
| a right-mover, **equal** to the newcomer | a left-mover | yes | **both** are destroyed | **stop, and do not join** |
| a right-mover, **heavier** than the newcomer | a left-mover | yes | the newcomer is destroyed | **stop, and do not join** |

Three of those five rows are "one comparison, one of three outcomes". The other two are the
no-collision shortcut. Everything below is a different way of executing this same table.

---

## Approach 1 — Sweep the lane until nothing changes

### The idea

*How do I know the lane has settled?* Look for any adjacent pair that would crash, resolve exactly that
one, and start looking again from the beginning. When a complete pass finds nothing to do, nothing can
happen, and that is the definition of settled.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** You are a traffic officer walking the length of a jam, and your only skill is
> resolving one crash. Walk from the front; the first crash you see, you settle; then — because
> removing a car has just made two other cars neighbours who were not neighbours before — you have no
> idea what your edit created behind you, so you walk back to the front and start over. The method is
> obviously correct precisely because it trusts nothing: it re-derives the whole state of the lane after
> every single change. That total distrust is also the entire cost.

### Worked example

`[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]`. State after every pass, with the pair the scan picked:

| pass | lane at the start of the pass | first colliding pair found | outcome | lane after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]` | `(2, -5)` at index 1 | 2 < 5 → top dies | `[10, -5, -12, 8, -8]` |
| 2 | `[10, -5, -12, 8, -8]` | `(10, -5)` at index 0 | 10 > 5 → incoming dies | `[10, -12, 8, -8]` |
| 3 | `[10, -12, 8, -8]` | `(10, -12)` at index 0 | 10 < 12 → top dies | `[-12, 8, -8]` |
| 4 | `[-12, 8, -8]` | `(8, -8)` at index 1 | equal → both die | `[-12]` |
| 5 | `[-12]` | none | — | `[-12]` — **settled** |

Five full scans of a six-element lane to resolve four collisions. Note pass 2: the pair `(10, -5)` did
not exist in the input at all. The `-5` became the `10`'s neighbour only because the `2` between them
was removed — that is the **cascade**, and it is why a single pass cannot possibly be enough.

### Code

```python
def asteroid_collision_sweep(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    current = list(asteroids)  # never mutate the caller's list
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(current) - 1):
            if not collides(current[i], current[i + 1]):
                continue
            verdict = outcome(current[i], current[i + 1])
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                current.pop(i)
            elif verdict == INCOMING_DIES:
                current.pop(i + 1)
            else:
                current.pop(i + 1)  # right index first, so the left one stays valid
                current.pop(i)
            changed = True
            break  # indices have moved; restart the scan
    return current
```

`collides` and `outcome` are the module-level helpers holding the case-analysis table. Every rung in
this document routes its comparison through them, so changing the rule is one edit in one place.

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** In the both-die case you will write `pop(i)` then `pop(i + 1)`, reading it as "remove
> the left one and the right one". After the first `pop`, **the right one is no longer at `i + 1`** —
> everything shifted down, so `i + 1` now names the element *after* the pair. You delete an innocent
> bystander and leave one of the colliders alive.

Run it. On `[4, -4, 7]` it returns `[-4]` instead of `[7]`: it removed the `4` and then the `7`. On
`[1, 2, 3, -3, -2, -1]` it returns `[-3, -1]` instead of `[]`. On the worked example and on the
statement's own `[8, -8]` it does not even return — it raises `IndexError: pop index out of range`,
because after removing one of two elements there is no index 1 left. Delete from the **right end
first** and both indices stay valid.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time `O(n²)`, space `O(n)`.** Each collision costs a restart, and a restart is a full scan — up to
`n` collisions × up to `n` steps each. The `pop(i)` itself shifts the tail, adding another `O(n)` per
collision, so the constant is worse than the bound suggests. Space is `O(n)` for the working copy.

Use it as the **oracle**. Its correctness argument is a single sentence — "it stops only when no pair
can collide, which is the definition of the answer" — and that makes it the reference the stress test
checks every faster rung against. At `n = 10⁴` it is roughly a hundred million element moves: too slow
to submit, fast enough to test with.

## Approach 2 — One pass, backing up one slot after each crash  *(an addition — not in the data file's ladder)*

### The idea

*The restart exists only because a crash might have created a new neighbour pair — but where can that
new pair be?* Only where the removal happened. So do not walk back to the front; step back **one**
slot and carry on.

This fixes Approach 1's weakness — **it rescans the entire prefix after every collision, even though a
removal at index `i` can only have created a new adjacency at `i − 1`.**

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** The same traffic officer, now willing to trust the part of the lane already behind
> him. After settling a crash he takes one step backwards — just far enough to see the pair his own
> edit created — and then resumes forward. The lane in front is untouched and the lane far behind is
> already known to be quiet, so one step back is exactly the right amount of distrust.

This rung matters because of what it *is*, not what it costs. Look at where the index spends its time:
it advances through quiet territory and retreats only into ground it has already cleared. The region to
the left of the index is a settled prefix that only ever shrinks from its right end. **That is a stack
wearing an array costume** — and noticing it is the whole step from here to the next rung. Backing up
one slot *is* popping.

### Worked example

`[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]`. The state is the working list plus the index `i`:

| step | `out` | `i` | pair at `(i, i+1)` | verdict | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]` | 0 | `(10, 2)` | no collision | `i → 1` |
| 2 | `[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]` | 1 | `(2, -5)` | top dies | `pop(1)`, `i → 0` |
| 3 | `[10, -5, -12, 8, -8]` | 0 | `(10, -5)` | incoming dies | `pop(1)`, `i → 0` |
| 4 | `[10, -12, 8, -8]` | 0 | `(10, -12)` | top dies | `pop(0)`, `i → 0` |
| 5 | `[-12, 8, -8]` | 0 | `(-12, 8)` | no collision | `i → 1` |
| 6 | `[-12, 8, -8]` | 1 | `(8, -8)` | both die | `pop(2)`, `pop(1)`, `i → 0` |
| 7 | `[-12]` | 0 | `i + 1` past the end | — | **stop** → `[-12]` |

Seven steps instead of five full passes, and steps 3 and 4 are the cascade being handled in place: the
index stayed at 0 and the `-12` kept fighting as new neighbours appeared.

### Code

```python
def asteroid_collision_resume(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = list(asteroids)
    i = 0
    while i + 1 < len(out):
        if not collides(out[i], out[i + 1]):
            i += 1
            continue
        verdict = outcome(out[i], out[i + 1])
        if verdict == TOP_DIES:
            out.pop(i)
        elif verdict == INCOMING_DIES:
            out.pop(i + 1)
        else:
            out.pop(i + 1)
            out.pop(i)
        i = max(i - 1, 0)  # the removal may have made out[i-1] and out[i] neighbours
    return out
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** You will drop the `i = max(i - 1, 0)` because the loop already looks like it covers
> every pair. It covers every pair **of the original list**. The pairs that matter are the ones your own
> deletions create, and those are always behind you.

Without the back-up, the worked example returns

```
[10, -5, -12]
```

instead of `[-12]` — three asteroids, two of which are a right-mover sitting immediately left of a
left-mover, which is a lane that has visibly not settled. The `-5` was removed from in front of the
`10` and the loop marched on without ever letting the `10` meet the `-12` behind it.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time `O(n²)` worst case, space `O(n)`.** The number of *comparisons* is now linear-ish — each step
either advances the index or destroys an asteroid, and there are only `n` of each — but every
`out.pop(i)` shifts the whole tail one slot left, and that is `O(n)` per collision. So the bound does
not actually improve; only the scanning half does. **That is the precise argument for the stack:** the
remaining `O(n²)` is entirely deletions from the middle of an array, and a structure that only ever
deletes from its end makes that cost vanish.

Use it when you want to demonstrate the idea without committing to an explicit stack, or when the
language makes middle-deletion cheap (a doubly-linked list). Mostly, use it as the rung that tells you
what to build next.

## Approach 3 — A stack of survivors

### The idea

*Which asteroid does an arriving left-mover meet first?* The most recently surviving right-mover — the
one nearest to it on the left. "Most recent survivor, removed first" is the definition of a stack, so
hold the survivors on one: push right-movers, and let a left-mover fight its way down.

This fixes Approach 2's weakness — **deleting from the middle of an array shifts everything after it**,
while the only deletions this problem ever needs are from the end.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** A stack of plates, and the plates are the asteroids that have survived so far. A
> right-mover is a plate you put down and stop thinking about. A left-mover is not a plate at all
> until it has proved it can survive: it arrives swinging, and it fights the top plate, then the next
> plate, then the next, for as long as those plates are right-movers smaller than it. It joins the
> stack only if it runs out of opponents — either the stack is empty or the top plate is itself a
> left-mover, which means it is driving away and will never be caught.

> **Why it works.** The invariant is that **the stack is always a settled lane**: read bottom to top it
> is a run of left-movers followed by a run of right-movers, so no positive ever sits immediately left
> of a negative inside it. Pushing a right-mover preserves this, because it lands on top of the
> right-mover run. Pushing a left-mover happens only when the stack is empty or its top is a left-mover
> — exactly when the left-mover run is what it lands on. And an arriving left-mover can only ever collide
> with the top, because everything below the top is shielded by it. So each asteroid is pushed at most
> once and popped at most once, and when the input is exhausted the stack is settled by construction —
> no final cleanup pass is needed or possible.

### Worked example

`[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]`. The state is the stack, bottom-to-top left-to-right:

| # | arriving | stack before | the fight | stack after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `10` | `[]` | right-mover — no fight | `[10]` |
| 2 | `2` | `[10]` | right-mover — no fight | `[10, 2]` |
| 3 | `-5` | `[10, 2]` | top `2` < 5 → **pop**, keep fighting; top `10` > 5 → **incoming dies** | `[10]` |
| 4 | `-12` | `[10]` | top `10` < 12 → **pop**, keep fighting; stack empty → survives | `[-12]` |
| 5 | `8` | `[-12]` | right-mover — no fight | `[-12, 8]` |
| 6 | `-8` | `[-12, 8]` | top `8` == 8 → **both die**; stop without pushing | `[-12]` |

Answer `[-12]`. Rows 3 and 4 are the cascade — one arrival, two comparisons — and row 6 is the case
that breaks naive code: the stack shrinks *and* the newcomer is discarded, which is the only row where
two things disappear at once. Total work: six arrivals, three pops, four collisions resolved — against
the five full scans the sweep needed.

### Code

```python
def asteroid_collision_stack(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    stack: list[int] = []
    for a in asteroids:
        alive = True  # does this newcomer still get to join?
        while alive and collides(stack[-1] if stack else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(stack[-1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                stack.pop()
                continue  # the newcomer fights on, against whatever is now on top
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                stack.pop()
            alive = False  # BOTH_DIE and INCOMING_DIES both end the newcomer's run
        if alive:
            stack.append(a)
    return stack
```

The `stack[-1] if stack else 0` reuses `collides` on an empty stack: `0` is a value the constraints
forbid for a real asteroid, and it collides with nothing, so the empty case falls out of the same
predicate instead of needing its own clause.

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** You will treat the equal case as "pop the top and carry on", because in the two other
> outcomes something survives and keeps going. Here **nothing** survives. The newcomer must leave the
> loop *and* skip the push, and a `continue` gives it neither.

```python
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                stack.pop()
                continue          # WRONG - the newcomer is dead but keeps fighting
```

On the statement's own `[8, -8]` that returns `[-8]` instead of `[]`: the `8` is correctly destroyed,
then the annihilated `-8` walks on, finds an empty stack, and is pushed as a survivor. On the worked
example it returns `[-12, -8]` instead of `[-12]`. The bug is invisible on any input with no equal
magnitudes, which is exactly why it survives a hand-check and dies on the hidden tests.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time `O(n)`, space `O(n)`.** Every asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the
total number of comparisons is bounded by `2n` no matter how long any individual fight runs — the inner
`while` looks quadratic and is not, because each of its iterations consumes a push that will never
happen again. Space is the stack, which in the worst case (`[1, 2, 3, …]`, nothing ever colliding)
holds all `n` elements.

**This is the one to write.** It is linear, it is fifteen lines, and its correctness is a single
invariant you can say out loud. Reach past it only when the caller can spare its input array, which is
the last rung.

## Approach 4 — The same stack, written with `break` / `else`  *(an addition — not in the data file's ladder)*

### The idea

*The `alive` flag exists only to carry "stop fighting" out of the loop and into the push decision — can
the control flow say that directly?* In Python, yes: `break` means "stopped early" and a `while`'s
`else` clause runs only when the loop was **not** broken out of, which is precisely "the newcomer never
lost".

This fixes no complexity weakness at all. It fixes a **readability** one: the flag is a second copy of
a fact the loop already knows, and two copies of one fact is where bugs live.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** Read `while … else` as *"fight; and if you were never stopped, take your place"*. The
> `break` is the newcomer dying — from either of the two ways of dying — and the `else` is the only path
> to the stack. The three outcomes of the case-analysis table map onto three keywords, one each:
> `continue` for "the top died, fight on", `break` for "the newcomer died", and `pop()` before the
> `break` for the case where both die.

The reason this is worth its own rung: with the flag, "do not push" is enforced by remembering to set a
variable, and forgetting is silent. With `break`/`else`, "do not push" is enforced by the control flow,
and there is no variable to forget. Same algorithm, one fewer thing that can go wrong.

### Worked example

Identical stack states to Approach 3 — it is the same algorithm — but tracking the keyword instead of
the flag:

| # | arriving | stack before | keyword taken | stack after | pushed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `10` | `[]` | loop never entered → `else` | `[10]` | yes |
| 2 | `2` | `[10]` | loop never entered → `else` | `[10, 2]` | yes |
| 3 | `-5` | `[10, 2]` | `pop` + `continue`, then `break` | `[10]` | **no** |
| 4 | `-12` | `[10]` | `pop` + `continue`, then loop condition fails → `else` | `[-12]` | yes |
| 5 | `8` | `[-12]` | loop never entered → `else` | `[-12, 8]` | yes |
| 6 | `-8` | `[-12, 8]` | `pop` + `break` | `[-12]` | **no** |

Row 4 is the subtle one and the reason `else` is the right clause: the loop ended because its
*condition* went false (the stack emptied), not because of a `break` — so `else` runs and the `-12` is
pushed. Row 3 ended with a `break`, so `else` is skipped. That single distinction is the whole
newcomer-survives question.

### Code

```python
def asteroid_collision_stack_break(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    stack: list[int] = []
    for a in asteroids:
        while collides(stack[-1] if stack else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(stack[-1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                stack.pop()
                continue
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                stack.pop()
            break  # the newcomer is destroyed - leave WITHOUT pushing
        else:
            stack.append(a)  # runs only when the loop ended without a break
    return stack
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** You will put `break` where `continue` belongs — after popping a smaller top — because
> "I destroyed something, I am done here" feels like the end of an interaction. It is not. Destroying
> the top is the one outcome where the newcomer **survives**, and a survivor keeps fighting.

```python
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                stack.pop()
                break             # WRONG - the newcomer won and should fight on
```

On the worked example that returns `[]` instead of `[-12]`. Trace why: the `-12` pops the `10`,
`break`s, and so skips the `else` — meaning it is neither destroyed nor pushed, it simply evaporates.
The bug looks like a survivor going missing, and the cause is the control flow saying "destroyed" when
the algorithm meant "victorious".

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time `O(n)`, space `O(n)`.** Identical to Approach 3 in every respect; the only thing that changed is
which construct carries the "did the newcomer survive" bit.

Use it in Python, where `while`/`else` is a real language feature and this is the idiomatic form. Use
the flag version in Java, C++, JavaScript, Go and everywhere else that has no loop-`else` — which is
exactly what the data file's Java and C++ solutions do, and why the flag version is the one worth
knowing in a language-agnostic interview.

## Approach 5 — The input array as its own stack  *(an addition — not in the data file's ladder)*

### The idea

*The stack only ever holds asteroids the walk has already passed — does it need its own memory?* No.
The survivors are always a subsequence of the input taken in order, and there are never more of them
than elements already read, so they can be written back over the front of the input array behind the
read position.

This fixes Approach 3's weakness — **an extra array of up to `n` elements** — at the cost of an
assumption the previous rungs did not need.

### What must be true, and what breaks without it

The assumption is that **the caller does not need its array afterwards**. That is often fine (LeetCode
gives you a fresh array; a pipeline stage may own its buffer) and sometimes catastrophic (the array is a
shared cache, a memory-mapped region, or a parameter the caller will read again). Nothing warns you:
the function returns the correct answer and the caller's data is simply gone.

The second thing that must be true is the index relationship, and it is worth checking rather than
trusting: `top`, the height of the stack, is never greater than the index currently being read.
Survivors are a subset of what has been read, so `top <= i` always, and the write at `asteroids[top]`
therefore lands on a slot already consumed — or, when `top == i`, writes an element back onto itself.
If that relationship failed anywhere, the algorithm would overwrite unread input and produce garbage.

### Worked example

`[10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]`. The state is the array itself plus `top`; everything at or past `top` is
stale leftovers, shown in parentheses:

| # | reading | `top` before | the fight | array after | `top` after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `10` | 0 | right-mover | `[10, (2, -5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 1 |
| 2 | `2` | 1 | right-mover | `[10, 2, (-5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 2 |
| 3 | `-5` | 2 | `2` < 5 → `top → 1`; `10` > 5 → incoming dies | `[10, (2, -5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 1 |
| 4 | `-12` | 1 | `10` < 12 → `top → 0`; empty → survives, written at 0 | `[-12, (2, -5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 1 |
| 5 | `8` | 1 | top is a left-mover — no fight, written at 1 | `[-12, 8, (-5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 2 |
| 6 | `-8` | 2 | `8` == 8 → `top → 1`, both die | `[-12, (8, -5, -12, 8, -8)]` | 1 |
| — | — | 1 | `del asteroids[1:]` | `[-12]` | 1 |

Step 4 is the one to look at: `top` was 1 and the read index was 3, so writing the `-12` at slot 0
overwrote the `10` — an element already consumed. No unread input is ever touched.

### Code

```python
def asteroid_collision_in_place(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Destroys the caller's list. asteroids[:top] is the stack; top <= the read index."""
    top = 0
    for a in asteroids:
        alive = True
        while alive and collides(asteroids[top - 1] if top else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(asteroids[top - 1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                top -= 1
                continue
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                top -= 1
            alive = False
        if alive:
            asteroids[top] = a
            top += 1
    del asteroids[top:]  # drop the stale tail; the stack is the whole answer
    return asteroids
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** You will forget `del asteroids[top:]`, because `top` feels like it *is* the answer once
> the loop ends. It is only the answer's **length**. Everything past it is whatever the algorithm
> happened to leave lying there — a mixture of original input and overwritten survivors.

On the worked example the untruncated version returns

```
[-12, 8, -5, -12, 8, -8]
```

instead of `[-12]`. The first element is right, which is what makes this pass a spot-check; the rest is
debris, including a duplicate `-12` that exists both as a survivor at slot 0 and as unconsumed input at
slot 3. The same bug wearing a different hat is returning `top` instead of the list — correct for a
problem that asks for a length, a silent disaster for one that asks for the contents.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time `O(n)`, space `O(1)`** extra. Same push-once-pop-once accounting as Approach 3; the space is
now a single integer, because the "stack" lives in storage the caller already allocated. The `del` at
the end is `O(1)` amortised in CPython — it only adjusts the length.

Use it when memory is the scarce resource and the input is genuinely yours: embedded work, a hot loop
over many arrays, or a streaming stage that owns its buffer. Do **not** use it as a default. Destroying
a caller's input to save an array that is at most `n` small integers is a bad trade almost everywhere,
and the bug it causes appears far away from this function, in whoever read the array next.

---

## The Overall Arc

Every rung here chases one principle: **resolve each collision at the moment it becomes possible,
instead of searching for it afterwards.** The repeated sweep sits at the far end of that — it has no
memory whatsoever, so after resolving one crash it throws away everything it knew about the lane and
re-derives it from the front, paying a full pass per collision and arriving at `O(n²)` for a problem
whose answer is a single subsequence. The first honest improvement is to notice that a deletion can only
create one new adjacency, exactly where the deletion happened, so stepping back one slot is enough
distrust; that halves the conceptual waste and exposes something more interesting, because the index
now only ever retreats into ground it has already cleared, which means the region to its left is a
settled prefix that grows at the right end and shrinks at the right end — a stack in an array costume,
still paying `O(n)` per deletion only because it is deleting from the middle of a list. Making the stack
explicit is therefore not a new idea but the same idea with the right container: push right-movers,
because nothing behind them can ever catch them, and let an arriving left-mover fight down through the
top, which is the only asteroid it can reach. From there the entire problem is the case-analysis table —
top lighter, keep fighting; top heavier, the newcomer dies; equal, both die and the newcomer must leave
without joining — and that third row is where nearly every wrong solution lives, because it is the only
outcome in which two things vanish at once and the only one where "stop" and "do not push" have to
happen together. Writing it with `break`/`else` rather than a liveness flag does not change a single
operation, but it moves that requirement from something you must remember into something the control
flow enforces. The last rung stops improving the algorithm and improves the storage: survivors are
always a subsequence of what has already been read, so the stack fits inside the input array behind the
read pointer, trading the caller's data for `O(1)` extra space — a constraint-exploiting trade that is
right in embedded code and wrong almost everywhere else. Rescan everything, rescan a little, rescan
nothing, say "rescan nothing" in the control flow, and finally store nothing — with the stack version
the one to know cold, and the sweep the one to keep, because it is the oracle that proved the others.

---

## Comparison

| Approach | Time | Space | Core trade-off | Best used when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sweep until settled | `O(n²)` | `O(n)` | Perfect distrust: re-derives the whole lane after each change, so correctness is obvious and cost is quadratic | You need an oracle for the stress test, or `n` is a handful |
| Back up one slot | `O(n²)` | `O(n)` | Scanning becomes linear, but deletions from the middle of an array keep the quadratic | A list with cheap middle deletion; as the step that reveals the stack |
| **Stack of survivors** | **`O(n)`** | **`O(n)`** | **Each asteroid pushed and popped once; needs a flag to carry "do not push"** | **The default answer, and the one to write in an interview** |
| Stack with `break`/`else` | `O(n)` | `O(n)` | Identical work; the control flow enforces "do not push" instead of a flag you must set | Python, where loop-`else` exists and reads as prose |
| Input array as the stack | `O(n)` | `O(1)` | Removes the auxiliary array by **destroying the caller's input** | Memory-bound code that genuinely owns its buffer |

---

## Interview Priority

**Know cold — the stack of survivors.** Linear, fifteen lines, and the only version worth submitting.
Be able to state the invariant without hesitating: the stack is always a settled lane, left-movers below
and right-movers above, so an arriving left-mover can only ever meet the top.

> **In an interview.** Write the five-row case-analysis table on the board **before** writing any code,
> and say why: three outcomes for a real collision, two shapes that cannot collide at all. Then say the
> sentence that earns the job — *"the equal case destroys both, so the newcomer stops fighting and is not
> pushed"* — because that is the line the interviewer is listening for, and the one most candidates only
> discover when a test fails. The follow-up is always the complexity of the inner `while`; answer that it
> is amortised, since each iteration consumes a push that can never happen again, so the total is bounded
> by `2n` however long a single fight runs.

**Know cold — the sweep-until-settled baseline.** Twenty seconds to describe, and it is what makes the
stack a **decision**. Say it, price it at `O(n²)`, name why it is wasteful — a full rescan per collision
when the only new adjacency is at the deletion point — and then improve it. Naming the cascade
(`[10, 2, -5]`, where one arrival causes two collisions) is what proves you understand why a single
left-to-right pass is not enough, and it is worth saying even though you will not write this version.

**Understand but do not memorize — the back-up-one-slot version.** Never the right code, since it keeps
the quadratic for a worse reason than the sweep does. Its value is one sentence: *the region behind the
index only ever grows and shrinks at its right end, which is a stack.* That observation is how you
**derive** the stack instead of recalling it, and it transfers directly to "remove adjacent duplicates",
"remove k digits" and every other neighbour-annihilation problem.

**Understand but do not memorize — `break`/`else` and the in-place variant.** One is a Python idiom that
will not survive translation to Java; the other is a space optimisation whose precondition (you may
destroy the input) is usually false and, when unstated, is a bug waiting in someone else's function.
Mention the in-place version as an available trade — *"`O(1)` extra if I may overwrite the input"* — and
let the interviewer decide.

## The same ladder, in Python, Java and C++

The explanation above works in Python. This is the app's own ladder for this
problem — the approaches it teaches, in build order — with every rung in all
three languages. Where the two differ, the explanation above may carry extra
rungs; each is labelled where it appears.


---

## Rung 1 — Sweep until nothing changes

Scan the list for an adjacent pair that would collide, resolve that one pair, and start over — repeating until a full scan finds nothing to do.

```python
def asteroid_collision(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    current = list(asteroids)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(current) - 1):
            if current[i] > 0 and current[i + 1] < 0:
                left, right = current[i], -current[i + 1]
                if left < right:
                    current.pop(i)
                elif left > right:
                    current.pop(i + 1)
                else:
                    current.pop(i + 1)
                    current.pop(i)
                changed = True
                break
    return current
```

**O(n²) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] asteroidCollision(int[] asteroids) {
    List<Integer> current = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int a : asteroids) current.add(a);
    boolean changed = true;
    while (changed) {
        changed = false;
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < current.size(); i++) {
            if (current.get(i) > 0 && current.get(i + 1) < 0) {
                int left = current.get(i);
                int right = -current.get(i + 1);
                if (left < right) {
                    current.remove(i);
                } else if (left > right) {
                    current.remove(i + 1);
                } else {
                    current.remove(i + 1);
                    current.remove(i);
                }
                changed = true;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    int[] out = new int[current.size()];
    for (int i = 0; i < out.length; i++) out[i] = current.get(i);
    return out;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> asteroidCollision(const vector<int>& asteroids) {
    vector<int> current = asteroids;
    bool changed = true;
    while (changed) {
        changed = false;
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < (int)current.size(); i++) {
            if (current[i] > 0 && current[i + 1] < 0) {
                int left = current[i];
                int right = -current[i + 1];
                if (left < right) {
                    current.erase(current.begin() + i);
                } else if (left > right) {
                    current.erase(current.begin() + i + 1);
                } else {
                    current.erase(current.begin() + i + 1);
                    current.erase(current.begin() + i);
                }
                changed = true;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    return current;
}
```

## Rung 2 — The one to remember

> **Why now.** Sweeping the list repeatedly until nothing changes is correct but pays a whole pass for each collision, and a chain of them makes that quadratic. A stack makes the opponent explicit: the asteroid a newcomer meets is always the one on top, so every collision is resolved the moment it becomes possible and each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once.

Walk left to right holding the survivors on a stack. A right-mover is simply pushed. A left-mover fights: while the top of the stack is a right-mover smaller than it, pop — those are destroyed. If the top is equal, both are destroyed and the newcomer stops. If the top is larger, the newcomer is destroyed. Only if the stack empties, or its top is itself a left-mover, does the newcomer survive and get pushed. The three outcomes of one comparison — pop and continue, both die, newcomer dies — are the whole problem.

```python
def asteroid_collision(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    stack: list[int] = []
    for a in asteroids:
        alive = True
        while alive and a < 0 and stack and stack[-1] > 0:
            if stack[-1] < -a:
                stack.pop()
                continue
            if stack[-1] == -a:
                stack.pop()
            alive = False
        if alive:
            stack.append(a)
    return stack
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] asteroidCollision(int[] asteroids) {
    List<Integer> stack = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int a : asteroids) {
        boolean alive = true;
        while (alive && a < 0 && !stack.isEmpty() && stack.get(stack.size() - 1) > 0) {
            int top = stack.get(stack.size() - 1);
            if (top < -a) {
                stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);
                continue;
            }
            if (top == -a) stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);
            alive = false;
        }
        if (alive) stack.add(a);
    }
    int[] out = new int[stack.size()];
    for (int i = 0; i < out.length; i++) out[i] = stack.get(i);
    return out;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> asteroidCollision(const vector<int>& asteroids) {
    vector<int> stack;
    for (int a : asteroids) {
        bool alive = true;
        while (alive && a < 0 && !stack.empty() && stack.back() > 0) {
            if (stack.back() < -a) {
                stack.pop_back();
                continue;
            }
            if (stack.back() == -a) stack.pop_back();
            alive = false;
        }
        if (alive) stack.push_back(a);
    }
    return stack;
}
```

</details>

---

## The arc

The narrative version is **The Overall Arc**, above. In one line:

> The stack is holding survivors, and the whole problem is a case analysis that must be written before any code: a right-moving asteroid always survives for now, a left-moving one fights everything right-moving on the stack, and each fight either destroys the incoming one, the stack top, or both.

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sweep until nothing changes | O(n²) time · O(n) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(n) space | Sweeping the list repeatedly until nothing changes is correct but pays a whole pass for each collision, and a chain of them makes that quadratic. A stack makes the opponent explicit: the asteroid a newcomer meets is always the one on top, so every collision is resolved the moment it becomes possible and each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once. |

## Full Runnable Script

The same five functions, assembled on the shared case-analysis helpers, plus a test suite: all three
statement examples, the worked example, the smallest legal input, both no-collision shapes, total
annihilation, duplicate magnitudes, and 59 randomised stress cases at `n = 2..60` with deliberately small
magnitudes so cascades are common. Every approach receives its **own copy** of the input, because the
in-place rung destroys it. Every answer is additionally checked to be genuinely settled — no positive
immediately followed by a negative — so that a case where all five agree on the same *wrong* answer
would still be caught.

```python
"""Asteroids That Collide - every approach in one file, plus a self-checking test suite.

Run: python asteroid_collision_all.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random

# --- the case-analysis table, written once and shared by every approach ---------

TOP_DIES = "top"            # the right-mover already held is destroyed; newcomer fights on
INCOMING_DIES = "incoming"  # the arriving left-mover is destroyed
BOTH_DIE = "both"           # equal magnitudes annihilate; newcomer must NOT be kept


def collides(left: int, right: int) -> bool:
    """The only shape that can ever collide: a right-mover immediately left of a left-mover."""
    return left > 0 and right < 0


def outcome(top: int, incoming: int) -> str:
    """Resolve one collision. `top` moves right, `incoming` moves left."""
    if top < -incoming:
        return TOP_DIES
    if top == -incoming:
        return BOTH_DIE
    return INCOMING_DIES


def is_settled(lane: list[int]) -> bool:
    """Harness only: an answer is settled when no adjacent pair can still collide."""
    return not any(collides(lane[i], lane[i + 1]) for i in range(len(lane) - 1))


# --- 1. Sweep until nothing changes (the reference) -----------------------------

def asteroid_collision_sweep(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    current = list(asteroids)  # never mutate the caller's list
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(current) - 1):
            if not collides(current[i], current[i + 1]):
                continue
            verdict = outcome(current[i], current[i + 1])
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                current.pop(i)
            elif verdict == INCOMING_DIES:
                current.pop(i + 1)
            else:
                current.pop(i + 1)  # right index first, so the left one stays valid
                current.pop(i)
            changed = True
            break  # indices have moved; restart the scan
    return current


# --- 2. One pass, backing up one slot after each collision ----------------------

def asteroid_collision_resume(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = list(asteroids)
    i = 0
    while i + 1 < len(out):
        if not collides(out[i], out[i + 1]):
            i += 1
            continue
        verdict = outcome(out[i], out[i + 1])
        if verdict == TOP_DIES:
            out.pop(i)
        elif verdict == INCOMING_DIES:
            out.pop(i + 1)
        else:
            out.pop(i + 1)
            out.pop(i)
        i = max(i - 1, 0)  # the removal may have made out[i-1] and out[i] neighbours
    return out


# --- 3. A stack of survivors, with a liveness flag ------------------------------

def asteroid_collision_stack(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    stack: list[int] = []
    for a in asteroids:
        alive = True  # does this newcomer still get to join?
        while alive and collides(stack[-1] if stack else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(stack[-1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                stack.pop()
                continue  # the newcomer fights on, against whatever is now on top
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                stack.pop()
            alive = False  # BOTH_DIE and INCOMING_DIES both end the newcomer's run
        if alive:
            stack.append(a)
    return stack


# --- 4. The same stack written with break / else --------------------------------

def asteroid_collision_stack_break(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    stack: list[int] = []
    for a in asteroids:
        while collides(stack[-1] if stack else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(stack[-1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                stack.pop()
                continue
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                stack.pop()
            break  # the newcomer is destroyed - leave WITHOUT pushing
        else:
            stack.append(a)  # runs only when the loop ended without a break
    return stack


# --- 5. The input array as its own stack ----------------------------------------

def asteroid_collision_in_place(asteroids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Destroys the caller's list. asteroids[:top] is the stack; top <= the read index."""
    top = 0
    for a in asteroids:
        alive = True
        while alive and collides(asteroids[top - 1] if top else 0, a):
            verdict = outcome(asteroids[top - 1], a)
            if verdict == TOP_DIES:
                top -= 1
                continue
            if verdict == BOTH_DIE:
                top -= 1
            alive = False
        if alive:
            asteroids[top] = a
            top += 1
    del asteroids[top:]  # drop the stale tail; the stack is the whole answer
    return asteroids


# --- harness -------------------------------------------------------------------

APPROACHES = [
    ("sweep", asteroid_collision_sweep),
    ("resume", asteroid_collision_resume),
    ("stack", asteroid_collision_stack),
    ("stack_break", asteroid_collision_stack_break),
    ("in_place", asteroid_collision_in_place),
]

NAMED_CASES: list[tuple[str, list[int]]] = [
    ("statement example 1", [5, 10, -5]),
    ("statement example 2", [8, -8]),
    ("statement example 3", [10, 2, -5]),
    ("worked example", [10, 2, -5, -12, 8, -8]),
    ("smallest legal input", [1, -1]),
    ("nothing ever collides", [-2, -1, 1, 2]),
    ("everything annihilates", [1, 2, 3, -3, -2, -1]),
    ("one arrival clears the stack", [1, 2, 3, 4, -5]),
    ("duplicate magnitudes", [4, 4, 4, -4]),
    ("all right-movers", [1, 2, 3]),
    ("all left-movers", [-1, -2, -3]),
]


def main() -> None:
    cases = list(NAMED_CASES)
    rng = random.Random(20260912)
    for n in range(2, 61):
        # small magnitudes make collisions - and cascades - common
        cases.append((f"stress n={n}", [rng.choice([-1, 1]) * rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]))

    width = max(len(name) for name, _ in APPROACHES)
    all_agreed = True

    for label, asteroids in cases:
        results = [fn(list(asteroids)) for _, fn in APPROACHES]  # each gets its OWN copy
        agreed = all(r == results[0] for r in results)
        settled = all(is_settled(r) for r in results)
        if not label.startswith("stress"):
            print(f"\n{label}: {asteroids}")
            for (name, _), got in zip(APPROACHES, results):
                print(f"  {name:<{width}} -> {got}")
        if not agreed or not settled:
            all_agreed = False
            print(f"\n{label}: {asteroids}")
            for (name, _), got in zip(APPROACHES, results):
                print(f"  {name:<{width}} -> {got}")
            print(f"  DISAGREEMENT (agreed={agreed}, settled={settled})")

    print(
        f"\n{len(cases)} cases ({len(cases) - len(NAMED_CASES)} randomised), "
        f"{len(APPROACHES)} approaches."
    )
    print(
        "ALL APPROACHES AGREED ON EVERY CASE."
        if all_agreed
        else "MISMATCH: the approaches did NOT all agree."
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
